analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to manipulate the derivatives and swaps markets and lets regulators fine, ban, and be sued by victims of manipulation.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2009, referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Commodity Exchange Act to make it illegal to manipulate the swaps and derivatives markets or file false information about them, and would have given the Commodity Futures Trading Commission power to investigate, fine violators up to triple their gains, and bar them from trading. It also let private parties sue over swap-related manipulation. It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing or a vote, so it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who pay prices set in commodity and energy markets — gasoline, food, electricity — would benefit if manipulation of the swaps markets that influence those prices were illegal and enforced. Consumers of financial products priced off swaps, and honest market participants competing against manipulators, would also gain from a cleaner market. Victims of manipulation would gain a new right to sue for their damages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of fuel, food, and electricity

how_it_helps.text: It made it explicitly illegal to use any manipulative or deceptive device in connection with a swap or commodity contract, and illegal to file false or misleading information about swaps with the CFTC [S3].

It raised the stakes: civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 or triple the violator's monetary gain for manipulation, restitution for damaged customers, and the ability to bar violators from trading on registered exchanges [S3].
It gave private parties the right to sue over manipulative conduct involving swaps, and gave the CFTC subpoena power to compel testimony and records, including from overseas witnesses [S2], [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other financial firms that trade swaps and derivatives would pay through fines of up to triple their gains, trading bans, restitution to victims, and private lawsuits, plus the compliance burden of accurate reporting. Heavy speculators whose trading can move prices would face the greatest enforcement risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street swap dealers and traders

drawbacks.text: The bill's enforcement powers were broad: the CFTC could bring show-cause hearings on just three days' notice and bar a person from trading before final adjudication, raising fair-process concerns that opponents could legitimately raise [S3].

Penalties tied to 'triple the monetary gain' and open-ended market definitions could reach legitimate hedging by ordinary businesses unless the CFTC's rules drew careful lines; the bill left the details to regulations written within a year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real public benefits: a clear ban on manipulating swaps, bigger fines, and the power for victims to sue — all aimed at the largely unregulated derivatives market that helped fuel the 2008 crisis. The main cost falls on dealers and speculators who would face enforcement and lawsuits; the bill included procedural protections such as court review of CFTC orders [S3]. The trade-off favors the public, but the bill never got a hearing, so no committee debate ever weighed the costs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died without a hearing or vote when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on September 17, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S1], [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted, so the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

The bill would have given the Commodity Futures Trading Commission explicit power to charge manipulative or deceptive conduct involving swaps, fine violators up to $1,000,000 or triple their monetary gain, bar them from trading, and let private parties sue [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Derivatives dealers and swap traders are better off: the bill that would have exposed them to fines, trading bans, and private lawsuits never advanced, and the swap market stayed outside the CFTC's manipulation authority for this Congress.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1], [S5].

for.name: Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original co-sponsor at introduction [S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over derivatives
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or reported it out, keeping it from the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Financial industry and derivatives dealers
against.role: Wall Street swap dealers and end-users
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against sweeping new derivatives regulation during the 2009-2010 financial reform debate, including expanded CFTC authority over the swaps market.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsor and five cosponsors were Democrats and an Independent, but since no vote ever occurred the record shows only that it drew no Republican support; the decisive inaction was in committee.

industries.industry: Derivatives dealers and swap traders (major banks)
industries.note: The bill made swap manipulation and false reporting unlawful, with fines up to $1 million or triple the violator's gain, trading bans, and private lawsuits — costs the largely unregulated swap market did not previously bear [S3]. Its death preserved the pre-reform legal environment for these firms.

industries.industry: Commodity and energy futures market users (airlines, food producers, energy firms)
industries.note: Hedgers who buy fuel, grain, and metals in derivatives markets would benefit from prices set by genuine supply and demand rather than manipulation; the bill protected them at no direct cost [S2].

The bill handed the CFTC explicit authority over the multi-trillion-dollar swap market, expanding its jurisdiction and enforcement toolkit [S2], [S3]. Its death left the agency's authority unresolved until Dodd-Frank later that Congress.
